p.src: Our destination is energy conservation, but first there is a correction to make. In the previous discussion of motion in polar coordinates, the outward term in the radial equation was called Coriolis. The correct name is centrifugal. Rather than repair only the word, we shall reconstruct the whole example. It provides the simplest route from the Euler–Lagrange equations to symmetry, conservation laws, and finally the Hamiltonian.

p.src: A Particle in Polar Coordinates

u.src: A Particle in Polar Coordinates
en: A Particle in Polar Coordinates

p.src: The working procedure is straightforward. Choose coordinates that describe the system, write the kinetic and potential energies, form the Lagrangian, and apply the Euler–Lagrange equations. The difficult part is usually choosing a good description; after that, the calculation is largely systematic.

p.src: For a particle moving in a plane, Cartesian coordinates $x,y$ are possible, but polar coordinates $r,\theta$ are better adapted to a force directed toward or away from an origin. The radial velocity is $v_r=\dot r,$ whereas the transverse velocity is $v_\theta=r\dot\theta.$ The factor of $r$ matters. At the same angular velocity, a point farther from the origin sweeps out a larger distance in the same time.

en: For a particle moving in a plane, Cartesian coordinates $x,y$ are possible, but polar coordinates $r,\theta$ are better adapted to a force directed toward or away from an origin. The radial velocity is $v_r=\dot r,$ whereas the transverse velocity is $v_\theta=r\dot\theta.$ The factor of $r$ matters. At the same angular velocity, a point farther from the origin sweeps out a larger distance in the same time.

p.src:
The two velocity components are perpendicular, so $v^2=\dot r^{\,2}+r^2\dot\theta^{\,2},$ and the kinetic energy is $T=\frac{m}{2}\left(\dot r^{\,2}+r^2\dot\theta^{\,2}\right).$ We now choose a central potential, $U=U(r),$ and therefore $\mathcal L
 =\frac{m}{2}\left(\dot r^{\,2}+r^2\dot\theta^{\,2}\right)-U(r).$ This restriction is not compulsory. A potential may depend on $\theta$, but then the system distinguishes one direction from another. Independence from $\theta$ is precisely rotational symmetry.

p.src: The first term on the right is positive in the outward radial direction. It is the centrifugal contribution. p.src: Rotational Symmetry and Angular Momentum

u.src: Rotational Symmetry and Angular Momentum
en: Rotational Symmetry and Angular Momentum

p.src:
The equation for $\theta$ is even more revealing. Its canonical momentum is $\pi_\theta
 =\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\dot\theta}
 =mr^2\dot\theta.$ Since $\theta$ does not occur in Eq. , $\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\theta}=0,$ and the angular Euler–Lagrange equation becomes $\frac{d}{dt}\left(mr^2\dot\theta\right)=0.$ Thus $mr^2\dot\theta=L,
 \qquad L=\text{constant}.$ The momentum conjugate to the angle is the angular momentum. Its value is not fixed by the law itself; it is fixed by the initial position and velocity. By contrast, $\pi_r=m\dot r$ generally changes because the radial force is not zero.

p.src: The effective radial equation at 00:21:10. Once the angular momentum is fixed, angular motion contributes the outward term $L^2/(mr^3)$.

u.src: The effective radial equation at 00:21:10. Once the angular momentum is fixed, angular motion contributes the outward term $L^2/(mr^3)$.

caption.en: The effective radial equation at 00:21:10. Once the angular momentum is fixed, angular motion contributes the outward term $L^2/(mr^3)$.

p.src:
The whole influence of the angular coordinate has now become an outward force proportional to $1/r^3$. Far from the origin it is weak; close to the origin it becomes very strong. It may also be written as the derivative of an effective potential, $m\ddot r=-\frac{dU_{\mathrm{eff}}}{dr},
 \qquad
 U_{\mathrm{eff}}(r)=U(r)+\frac{L^2}{2mr^2}.$ The second term is the centrifugal barrier.

p.src: For gravity or the Coulomb force, the attractive force varies as $1/r^2$, whereas the centrifugal contribution varies as $1/r^3$. At sufficiently small $r$, nonzero angular momentum therefore wins. This is why an orbiting planet does not simply crash into the central body. If the motion is exactly radial, however, then $L=0$, the barrier disappears, and a collision may occur.

p.src: Variations and Stationarity

u.src: Variations and Stationarity
en: Variations and Stationarity

p.src:
We need one piece of notation before turning to the general theorem. Let $F$ be a function of many variables $\alpha_i$. Under small changes $\delta\alpha_i$, its first-order change is $\delta F
 =\sum_i\frac{\partial F}{\partial\alpha_i}\,\delta\alpha_i
 +O(\delta\alpha^2).$ If $\delta F=0$ for every independent choice of $\delta\alpha_i$, then $\frac{\partial F}{\partial\alpha_i}=0
 \qquad\text{for every }i.$ This is the meaning of stationarity to first order. A minimum is stationary, but stationarity is the precise property needed in the action principle.

p.src:
For a trajectory the same shorthand becomes $A[q]=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\mathcal L(q,\dot q,t)\,dt,
 \qquad \delta A=0.$ The variation of the action is $\delta A
 =\int_{t_1}^{t_2}
 \sum_i\left(
 \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial q_i}\,\delta q_i
 +\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\dot q_i}\,\delta\dot q_i
 \right)dt.$ This notation is not an additional physical principle. It is a compact way of collecting all first-order changes.

p.src: Continuous Symmetries

u.src: Continuous Symmetries
en: Continuous Symmetries

p.src: A symmetry is a transformation that leaves the action unchanged. Translating an isolated system is a symmetry when the action depends only on relative positions. Rotating a rotationally invariant system is another. In each case the transformation acts on the entire history, not merely on one particle at one instant.

Rotating a rotationally invariant system is another. In each case the transformation acts on the entire history, not merely on one particle at one instant.
en: A symmetry is a transformation that leaves the action unchanged. Translating an isolated system is a symmetry when the action depends only on relative positions. Rotating a rotationally invariant system is another. In each case the transformation acts on the entire history, not merely on one particle at one instant.

p.src:
We shall study continuous symmetries through infinitesimal transformations, $q_i\longrightarrow q_i+\epsilon f_i(q),
 \qquad
 \delta q_i=\epsilon f_i(q),$ where $\epsilon$ is small. The displacement may depend on the point in configuration space. A finite translation or rotation can be built from many small ones, so first-order information is sufficient.

en:
We shall study continuous symmetries through infinitesimal transformations, $q_i\longrightarrow q_i+\epsilon f_i(q),
 \qquad
 \delta q_i=\epsilon f_i(q),$ where $\epsilon$ is small. The displacement may depend on the point in configuration space. A finite translation or rotation can be built from many small ones, so first-order information is sufficient.

p.src:
For an infinitesimal counterclockwise rotation in the $x$-$y$ plane, $\delta x=-\epsilon y,
 \qquad
 \delta y=\epsilon x,$ and therefore $f_x=-y,
 \qquad f_y=x.$ The signs can be checked on the axes. At a point on the positive $x$-axis, $y=0$, so $x$ does not change to first order while $y$ increases. At a point on the positive $y$-axis, $x$ decreases while $y$ does not change to first order.

p.src: Noether’s Theorem

u.src: Noether’s Theorem
en: Noether’s Theorem

p.src: Begin with a trajectory $q_i(t)$ that satisfies the equations of motion. An ordinary least-action variation keeps its endpoints fixed. A symmetry variation is different: it transforms every point of the trajectory, including the endpoints. The action still does not change, but now it vanishes for a different reason. It vanishes because the transformation is a symmetry, not because it belongs to the fixed-endpoint family used to derive the equations of motion.

It vanishes because the transformation is a symmetry, not because it belongs to the fixed-endpoint family used to derive the equations of motion.

p.src:
Integrating the second term of Eq.  by parts gives $\begin{aligned}
 \delta A
 &={}
 \int_{t_1}^{t_2}\sum_i
 \left[
 \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial q_i}
 -\frac{d}{dt}\left(
   \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\dot q_i}
  \right)
 \right]\delta q_i\,dt \\
 &\quad+
 \left[
 \sum_i\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\dot q_i}\,
 \delta q_i
 \right]_{t_1}^{t_2}.
 \end{aligned}$ The bulk integral vanishes because the original path obeys the Euler–Lagrange equations. The boundary term does not vanish by an endpoint condition, because the symmetry moved those endpoints. Instead symmetry tells us that the full $\delta A$ vanishes. Consequently, $\left[
 \sum_i\pi_i\,\delta q_i
 \right]_{t_1}^{t_2}=0.$ Substitute Eq.  and remove the common constant $\epsilon$: $\left[Q\right]_{t_1}^{t_2}=0,
 \qquad
 Q=\sum_i\pi_i f_i(q).$ Since the endpoints may be any two times, $\frac{dQ}{dt}=0.$

p.src: This is Noether’s theorem in the form needed here. The quantity $Q$ is called the Noether charge. The word charge is used broadly: it means a conserved quantity, not necessarily electric charge. Momentum, angular momentum, and energy are all Noether charges. The theorem also uses two facts together: the equations arise from an action principle, and the action has a continuous symmetry. Invariance of an arbitrary equation, without an action principle, is not by itself this theorem.

p.src: Translation and Rotation Charges

u.src: Translation and Rotation Charges
en: Translation and Rotation Charges

p.src:
Consider a closed system of many particles. Under a common translation in the $x$-direction, $\delta x_a=\epsilon,
 \qquad
 \delta y_a=\delta z_a=0$ for every particle label $a$. Thus $f_{x_a}=1$, and Eq.  gives $Q_x=\sum_a\pi_{x_a}=\sum_a m_a\dot x_a
 =\sum_a p_{x_a}.$ The conserved Noether charge is total momentum in the translation direction. The detailed internal forces were never needed. We required only that moving the whole isolated system leave its potential energy unchanged. A fixed external body would spoil that symmetry unless it too were included in the dynamical system.

p.src: Once a candidate symmetry is known, constructing its charge is mechanical: find the infinitesimal generator $f_i$, multiply by the corresponding canonical momenta, and sum. Finding all the symmetries of a complicated system may be difficult; using Noether’s formula after finding one is not.

p.src: Time Translation

u.src: Time Translation
en: Time Translation

p.src: Suppose the laws and external conditions have no explicit dependence on time. If one solution is begun a little later, the displaced history is again a solution. An orbit does not care whether we label a particular state as eleven o’clock or one minute later; the whole orbit is merely shifted in time. This is time-translation invariance.

p.src: The qualification about external conditions is essential. If we study only part of a system while a massive external body moves according to a prescribed schedule, the forces on our subsystem depend explicitly on time. Translating only the subsystem’s history is then not a symmetry.

p.src:
Let the original trajectory be $q_i(t)$. Pushing it forward in time by $\epsilon$ gives the new function $q_i^{(\epsilon)}(t)=q_i(t-\epsilon).$ At a fixed value of $t$, the induced displacement in configuration space is $\begin{aligned}
 \delta q_i(t)
 &=q_i(t-\epsilon)-q_i(t) \\
 &=-\epsilon\dot q_i(t)+O(\epsilon^2).
 \end{aligned}$

p.src: The Endpoint Overhangs

u.src: The Endpoint Overhangs
en: The Endpoint Overhangs

p.src: A time translation is not quite an ordinary symmetry of configuration space: it also shifts the interval over which the action is evaluated. Draw the original trajectory and its translate with time running vertically. Through most of the interval they overlap, but the translated path leaves one short extra segment at the upper endpoint while the original leaves one at the lower endpoint. These short segments are the overhangs.

 \right]_{t_1}^{t_2}
 =-\epsilon
 \left[
 \sum_i\pi_i\dot q_i
 \right]_{t_1}^{t_2}.$ The bulk term again vanishes on the equations of motion.

p.src: The upper overhang lasts for the small time $\epsilon$, so its action is, to first order, $A_{\mathrm{upper}}=\epsilon\mathcal L(t_2)+O(\epsilon^2).$ Similarly, the lower overhang contributes $A_{\mathrm{lower}}=\epsilon\mathcal L(t_1)+O(\epsilon^2).$ This approximation assumes that $\mathcal L$ is regular and changes little over a sufficiently short interval. No singular behavior is being allowed at the endpoints.

p.src:
Time-translation symmetry says that the total action difference is zero. Combining the ordinary boundary term with the two overhangs gives $0=\epsilon
 \left[
 \mathcal L-\sum_i\pi_i\dot q_i
 \right]_{t_1}^{t_2}.$ Therefore $\mathcal L-\sum_i\pi_i\dot q_i
 =\text{constant}.$

p.src: The Hamiltonian Is the Energy

u.src: The Hamiltonian Is the Energy
en: The Hamiltonian Is the Energy

p.src: The conserved expression has first appeared with the opposite sign from the usual convention. The negative of a conserved quantity is also conserved, so we define $H=\sum_i\pi_i\dot q_i-\mathcal L.$ This is the Hamiltonian, and it is the Noether charge associated with time translation.

en: The conserved expression has first appeared with the opposite sign from the usual convention. The negative of a conserved quantity is also conserved, so we define $H=\sum_i\pi_i\dot q_i-\mathcal L.$ This is the Hamiltonian, and it is the Noether charge associated with time translation.

p.src:
For a one-dimensional particle with $\mathcal L=\frac12m\dot x^2-U(x),$ the canonical momentum is $\pi_x=m\dot x$, and therefore $\begin{aligned}
 H
 &=\pi_x\dot x-\mathcal L \\
 &=m\dot x^2-\left(\frac12m\dot x^2-U(x)\right) \\
 &=\frac12m\dot x^2+U(x).
 \end{aligned}$ Thus, for the familiar Lagrangian $T-U$, the Hamiltonian is the familiar energy $T+U$.

p.src: Regularity and explicit time dependence

u.src: Regularity and explicit time dependence
en: Regularity and explicit time dependence

p.src: If the Lagrangian depends explicitly on time, $\mathcal L=\mathcal L(q,\dot q,t),$ then shifting a trajectory in time need not leave the action invariant. The derivation above no longer gives a conservation law, and energy need not be conserved. The precise evolution law for that case will be developed after the Hamiltonian formalism is in place.

p.src: The compactness of the action is one reason this language became fundamental. The polar-coordinate equations contain centrifugal terms that would be awkward to guess directly, while the Lagrangian in Eq.  is easy to remember. The same economy persists in field theory, electromagnetism, relativity, and quantum theory. Lagrange’s formulation came first; Hamilton’s reformulation followed in the nineteenth century and became the natural bridge to quantum mechanics.

u.src: Symmetry and Dynamics in One View
en: Symmetry and Dynamics in One View

p.src: The polar-coordinate correction already contains the pattern of the whole chapter. Rotational invariance removes $\theta$ from the Lagrangian, so its conjugate momentum $L=mr^2\dot\theta$ is conserved. Substituting that constant into the radial equation exposes the centrifugal barrier $L^2/(mr^3)$.

p.src: The general pattern is Noether’s theorem. An infinitesimal symmetry $\delta q_i=\epsilon f_i(q)$ has the conserved charge $Q=\sum_i\pi_i f_i(q).$ Translations give momentum and rotations give angular momentum. Time translation requires one extra piece of bookkeeping because the integration interval moves. Its endpoint overhangs combine with the ordinary variational boundary term to give $H=\sum_i\pi_i\dot q_i-\mathcal L.$ The Hamiltonian is therefore not merely a convenient formula. It is the conserved charge that expresses the independence of the laws of physics from when an isolated experiment is performed.
